text: 薩摩守忠度は、いづくよりか歸られたりけん、侍五騎、童一人、我身共に七騎取て返し、五條の三位俊成卿の宿所におはして見給へば門戸をとぢて開かず。忠度と名乘給へば、落人歸り來たりとて、其内噪ぎあへり。薩摩守馬より下り、自高らかに宣ひけるは、「別の子細候はず、三位殿に申べき事有て、忠度が歸り參て候。門を開れず共、此際迄立寄らせ給へ。」と宣へば、俊成卿「さる事あるらん。其人ならば苦かるまじ。入れ申せ。」とて、門をあけて對面有り。事の體何となうあはれなり。薩摩守宣ひけるは、「年來申承はて後、愚ならぬ御事に思ひ參らせ候へ共、この二三年は京都の噪、國々の亂併當家の身の上の事に候間疎略を存せずといへども、常に參り寄る事も候はず。君既に都を出させ給ひぬ。一門の運命はや盡候ぬ。撰集の有るべき由承りしかば、生涯の面目に、一首なり共御恩を蒙らうと存じて候しに、やがて世の亂出で來て、其沙汰なく候條、唯一身の歎きと存ずる候。世靜まり候なば勅撰の御沙汰候はんずらん。是に候ふ卷物の中に、さりぬべきもの候はゞ、一首なりとも御恩を蒙て、草の蔭にても嬉しと存候はば、遠き御守りとこそ成參せ候んずれ。」とて、日來詠置れたる歌共の中に、秀歌と覺きを百餘首書集られたる卷物を、今はとて打立れける時、是を取て持れたりしが、鎧の引合せより取出でて、俊成卿に奉る。三位是をあけて見て、「かゝる忘れ形見を給り置候ぬる上は、努々疎略を存ずまじう候。御疑あるべからず。さても只今の御渡りこそ情も勝れて深う、哀れも殊に思ひしられて感涙抑へ難う候へ。」と宣へば、薩摩守悦で「今は西海の浪の底に沈まば沈め、山野に尸をさらさばさらせ、浮世に思置く事候はず。さらば暇申て。」とて、馬に打乘り、甲の緒をしめ、西を指いてぞ歩せ給ふ。三位後を遙に見送て立たれたれば、忠度の聲と覺しくて、「前途程遠し、思を雁山の夕の雲に馳。」と、高らかに口ずさみ給へば、俊成卿、いとゞ名殘惜しう覺えて、涙を抑てぞ入給ふ。其後世靜て、千載集を撰ぜられけるに、忠度のありし有樣、言置し言の葉、今更思出て哀なりければ、彼の卷物の中に、さりぬべき歌幾らもありけれど、勅勘の人なれば、名字をば顯されず、「故郷花」といふ題にて詠まれたりける歌一首ぞ、讀人しらずと入られける。

annotation.translation: Saemon no Kami Tadanori, having returned from somewhere, took with him five mounted samurai and one page, seven in all, and returned. When they arrived at the residence of Sanjo no Sanmi Shunsei no Kyo, they found the gate shut and barred. When Tadanori announced his name, they shouted that he was a fugitive who had returned. Saemon no Kami dismounted from his horse and loudly declared, "There is no special trouble; there is something I must tell Lord Sanjo. Tadanori has returned. Even if you do not open the gate, please allow me to wait here until this moment." Shunsei Kyo said, "If such a matter exists, and if it is he, there is no need for worry. Let him in." Thus the gate was opened, and they met. The circumstances were truly pitiful. Saemon no Kami declared, "After receiving your patronage over the years, I have often thought of you as a wise and noble person, yet for the past two or three years, due to the disturbances in Kyoto, the chaos in the provinces, and the plight of my own family, I have felt unable to visit you, though I did not intend to neglect you. Your Majesty has already left the capital. The fate of our entire house has come to an end. Upon hearing that there would be a new anthology compiled, I had resolved to receive your grace, even in a single poem, as a matter of my lifelong honor. However, the chaos of the world soon erupted, and thus I have nothing to report, so I have regarded it merely as a personal lament. If the world should become peaceful and an imperial anthology be compiled, if there should be something in this scroll that could be selected, even if it were a single poem, and if I could receive your grace and feel joy even in the shade of grass, then I would be truly grateful for your distant protection." At this moment, while he was about to set aside the scroll containing over one hundred poems that he had selected from those composed over the years and deemed excellent, he took it out from the clasp of his armor and presented it to Shunsei Kyo. Lord Sanjo opened it and read it, saying, "Since you have left such a cherished memento, I shall certainly not neglect it. There is no need for suspicion. Moreover, your journey just now was particularly moving and deeply poignant, and I am overwhelmed with emotion and cannot hold back my tears." Saemon no Kami, delighted, said, "Now, whether I sink to the bottom of the waves of the Western Sea or whether my corpse is left exposed in the mountains and fields, I have no lingering thoughts for this floating world. Then, I take my leave." Mounting his horse, tightening the straps of his armor, he pointed westward and walked away. Lord Sanjo stood watching him depart into the distance. Hearing his voice, which he recognized as Tadanori's, he thought, "The road ahead is so long; let my thoughts race to the evening clouds of the Goose Mountains." As he hummed this loudly, Shunsei Kyo felt an even deeper sense of lingering sorrow and, holding back his tears, entered the house. Later, when the world became peaceful and the Senzai Wakashu was compiled, remembering Tadanori's presence and his words brought great sorrow. Although there were many poems in that scroll that could have been selected, since he was a person under imperial censure, his name was not revealed; instead, a single poem titled "Flowers of My Hometown" was included, though no one knew the reader's name.

Then, I take my leave." Mounting his horse, tightening the straps of his armor, he pointed westward and walked away. Lord Sanjo stood watching him depart into the distance. Hearing his voice, which he recognized as Tadanori's, he thought, "The road ahead is so long; let my thoughts race to the evening clouds of the Goose Mountains." As he hummed this loudly, Shunsei Kyo felt an even deeper sense of lingering sorrow and, holding back his tears, entered the house. Later, when the world became peaceful and the Senzai Wakashu was compiled, remembering Tadanori's presence and his words brought great sorrow. Although there were many poems in that scroll that could have been selected, since he was a person under imperial censure, his name was not revealed; instead, a single poem titled "Flowers of My Hometown" was included, though no one knew the reader's name.

text: 修理大夫經盛の子息、皇后宮亮經正、幼少にては、仁和寺の御室の御所に、童形にて、候はれしかば、かゝる怱劇の中にも、其御名殘きと思出て、侍五六騎具して、仁和寺殿へ馳參り、門前にて馬より下り、申入られけるは、「一門運盡て今日既に帝都を罷出候。浮世に思ひ殘す事とては、唯君の御名殘計也。八歳の時參り始め候て、十三で元服仕り候し迄は、相勞る事の候はぬ外は、白地にも御前を立去事も候はざりしに、今日より後西海千里の浪路に趣いて、又何の日、何の時、歸り參るべしとも覺えぬこそ口惜う候へ。今一度御前へ參て、君をも見參せたう候へども、既に甲冑を鎧ひ弓箭を帶し、あらぬ樣なる粧に罷成て候へば、憚存候。」とぞ申されける。御室哀に思召し、「唯其姿を改めずして參れ。」とこそ仰せけれ。經正其日は、紫地の錦の直垂に、萠黄匂の鎧著て、長覆輪の太刀を帶き、切斑の矢負ひ、滋籘の弓脇に挾み、甲をば脱高紐にかけ、御前の御坪に畏る。御室やがて御出有て、御簾高く揚させ「是へ／＼」と召されければ、大床へこそ參られけれ。供に具せられたる藤兵衞有教を召す。赤地の錦の袋に入たる御琵琶持て參たり。經正是を取次で、御前にさし置き申されけるは、「先年下し預て候し青山持せて參て候。餘りに名殘は惜しう候へども、さしもの名物を、田舎の塵に成ん事口惜う候。若不思議に運命開けて、又都へ立歸る事候はゞ、其時こそ猶下し預り候はめ。」と泣々申されければ、御室哀におぼしめし一首の御詠をあそばいて下されけり。

annotation.translation: The son of Shuji no Daibu Kanesakira, Kagemasa, who served as the Chamberlain to the Empress, when still a young child, had been attending the Imperial Princess of Ninna-ji Temple in the capacity of a page. Thus, amidst such a crisis, feeling that he should not forget the Imperial Princess's favor, he equipped himself with five or six horsemen and rushed to the residence of the Prince of Ninna-ji Temple. There, dismounting before the gate, he reported: 'Our clan's fortune has ended; today we have already departed the capital. As for things I regret leaving behind in this fleeting world, it is only your Imperial Majesty's presence that I cannot bear to part with. From the time I first came to your service at the age of eight until I underwent my coming-of-age ceremony at thirteen, there was nothing I did not attend to with diligence; I never once left your presence, even on white ground. Yet from today onward, I shall journey along the thousand-ri sea waves of the Western Sea, and I have no notion of what day, what hour, or even if I shall ever return to the capital. This is deeply regrettable. If I could once more come before your Imperial Majesty to see you, I would do so with all my heart; however, I am now clad in armor, wearing a helmet, and girded with bow and arrows, having assumed a strange and unsuitable attire, which makes it impossible for me to approach.' Thus he spoke. The Imperial Princess, deeply grieved, commanded: 'Then, come as you are, without changing your appearance.' So she ordered him. That day, Kagemasa wore a violet-colored brocade hitatare, a lacquered armor dyed in the scent of sprouting yellow, a long-laced tachi at his waist, a cut-patterned quiver of arrows on his back, and a bamboo bow tucked at his side. He removed his armor and hung it on the high cord, then stood humbly before the Imperial Princess's courtyard. The Imperial Princess soon emerged from her quarters, raised her curtains high, and summoned him, saying, 'Come here, come here.' Thus he approached the great hall. He summoned Fujisuke no Iemasa, who had accompanied him. He brought a imperial biwa enclosed in a crimson brocade bag. Kagemasa took it and placed it before the Imperial Princess, saying: 'I have brought the green hill that was granted to me in previous years. Though I regret it exceedingly to part with such a famous treasure, I fear it will become dust in the countryside. If, by some miracle, fate should open a way for me to return to the capital, then at that time I shall surely be permitted to receive it again.' Thus he spoke, weeping. The Imperial Princess, moved to deep sorrow, composed a verse and bestowed it upon him.

text: さては暇申て出られけるに、數輩の童形、出世者、坊官、侍僧に至迄、經正の袂にすがり、袖を引へて、名殘を惜み、涙を流さぬは無りけり。其中にも經正幼少の時、小師でおはせし大納言法印行慶と申は、葉室大納言光頼卿の御子也。餘に名殘を惜みて、桂河の端迄打送り、さてもあるべきならねば其より暇請うて泣々別れ給ふに、法印かうぞ思續け給ふ。

annotation.translation: Thus, when he had taken his leave and departed, a multitude of young boys, high-ranking attendants, temple officials, and warrior monks, all the way to the priests, clung to Kyoza's sleeve, pulled at his hem, regretted the parting, and not a single one failed to shed tears. Among them, Kyoza's former teacher when he was a young boy was the Daigagon Hōin Gyokei, who was the son of the Daigagon Munechika of the Hamamatsu family. Grieving the parting all the more, they escorted him as far as the banks of the Katsura River; but since that was not something that could be done further, he asked for permission to depart from there and, with tears in his eyes, they took their sorrowful farewell. The Hōin then thought, 'This is indeed what I have been pondering.'

Even the servants who knew nothing would not have mistaken it for a village rain. These were joyful things.

text: 彼青山と申す御琵琶は、昔仁明天皇御宇、嘉祥三年の春、掃部頭貞敏渡唐の時、大唐の琵琶博士廉妾夫に逢ひ、三曲を傳へて歸朝せしに、玄象、獅子丸、青山、三面の琵琶を相傳して渡りけるが、龍神や惜み給ひけん、浪風荒く立ければ、獅子丸をば海底に沈めぬ。今二面の琵琶を渡して、吾朝の御門の御寶とす。

annotation.translation: This biwa called Aoyama, in the spring of the third year of Kashō, during the reign of Emperor Ninmyō, when Kanmuri-no-suke Sadatoshi traveled to Tang China, met the biwa master of the Great Tang, Renjofu, and was instructed in three pieces before returning to the court. He had crossed over with four biwas: Genzō, Shishimaru, Aoyama, and Sanmen, but the dragon god, pitying them, caused the waves and winds to rise wildly, so Shishimaru was sunk to the ocean floor. Now, two biwas were brought back and established as a treasure of our imperial court.

text: 村上聖代應和の比ほひ、三五夜中の新月白く冴え、凉風颯々たりし夜半に、御門清凉殿にして、玄象をぞ遊されける。時に影の如くなる者、御前に參じて、優にけだかき聲にて、唱歌を目出たう仕る。御門御琵琶を差置かせ給て、「抑汝は如何なる者ぞ。何くより來れるぞ。」と御尋あれば、「是は昔貞敏に三曲を傳へし大唐の琵琶博士、廉妾夫と申す者で候が、三曲の中、祕曲を一曲殘せるに依て、魔道に沈淪仕て候。今御琵琶の御撥音妙に聞えて侍る間、參入仕る處也。願くは此曲を君に授け奉り、佛果菩提を證すべき」由申て、御前に立られたる青山を取り、轉手をねぢて、祕曲を君に授け奉る。三曲の中に上玄、石上是也。其後は、君も臣も恐させ給て、此御琵琶を遊し彈く事もせさせ給はず、御室へ參せられたりけるを、經正の幼少の時御最愛の童形たるに依て、下し預りたりけるとかや。甲は紫藤の甲、夏山の嶺の緑の木間より、有明の月の出るを、撥面に書かれたりける故にこそ、青山とは附られたれ。玄象にも相劣らぬ希代の名物なりけり。

annotation.translation: In the time of Emperor Murakami, during the era of Engi, on the third and fifth nights of the new moon, the moon shone white and clear, and in the cool wind of the middle of the night, at the Imperial Gate, in the Seiryoden, the Emperor played the celestial phenomena. At that time, a being like a shadow appeared before him, and with a voice exceeding height, joyfully performed a song. The Emperor, having set aside his Imperial biwa, asked, "Pray, what manner of being are you? From where have you come?" When this was asked, the shadow replied, "I am the Tang biwa master, named Ren Shoufu, who once transmitted the Three Melodies to Teimin. Because I left one secret melody among the Three Melodies, I sank into the ways of demons. Now, as the sound of your Imperial biwa's plectrum is heard with exquisite beauty, I have come to enter. I pray that you grant me this melody, that I may attain the Buddha fruit and Bodhi." Having said this, he seized the green mountain standing before him, twisted his hand, and transmitted the secret melody to the Emperor. Among the Three Melodies, the upper mystery, Sekijo, is this. After that, both the Emperor and the ministers were terrified, and were not allowed to play or even touch this Imperial biwa, and it was taken to the Imperial chamber. However, because it was the most beloved object of Emperor Kōkō in his youth, it was given to and kept by him. The case is the wisteria case; because from the green trees of the summer mountain ridge, the moon of Arima was depicted on the plectrum face, it was named the Green Mountain. It was a rare treasure, no inferior to the celestial phenomena.

text: 池の大納言頼盛卿も、池殿に火を懸て出られけるが、鳥羽の南の門に引へつゝ、「忘たる事あり。」とて、赤印切捨て、其勢三百餘騎都へ取て歸られけり。平家の侍越中次郎兵衞盛嗣、大臣殿の御前に馳參て「あれ、御覽候へ、池殿の御留まり候に、多の侍共の付參らせて、罷留まるが、奇怪に覺え候。大納言殿迄は恐れも候、侍共に矢一つ射懸候はん。」と申ければ。「年比の重恩を忘て、今此有樣を見果ぬ不當人をば、さなくとも有なん。」と宣へば、力及ばで留まりけり。「さて小松殿の君達は如何に。」と宣へば「未御一所も見えさせ給はず。」と申す。其時、新中納言殿、涙をはらはらと流いて「都を出て未だ一日だにも過ざるに、何しか人の心共の變行くうたてさよ。まして行末とてもさこそはあらんずらめと思しかば都の内で如何にも成らんと、申つる者を。」とて、大臣殿の御方を、世にも恨げにこそ見給ひけれ。

annotation.translation: The Great Councilor Yoritomo of the Ikeda family, who had set fire to the Ikeda residence and fled, was being drawn back at the southern gate of Toba, saying, 'I have forgotten something.' He cut off the red seal, and with his force of over three hundred horsemen, took them back to the capital. Heike's retainer Chūnagon Jirō Bēemon Morihiro ran to the presence of the Minister and said, 'Look, Your Excellency, the Ikeda residence has been left behind with many of our retainers accompanying it, and it seems very strange. Even the Great Councilor has shown fear; our retainers might shoot an arrow.' To this, the Minister replied, 'Those who, forgetting the heavy favors of bygone years, now wish to see this state of affairs, are unworthy of even a little mercy.' With this, they were unable to restrain him and stayed. Then, 'How are the lords of Komatsu?' he asked. 'They have not yet even shown themselves to a single residence,' they replied. At that moment, the new Chancellor, with tears streaming down his face, said, 'It has not even been a day since we left the capital, yet how terrible the fickleness of human hearts! I thought that even our fate would surely be so, and thus, within the capital, things would turn out as they would, and I had spoken such words.' So, he looked at the Minister's side with a deep, worldly regret.

text: 抑池殿の留まり給ふ事を如何にと云に兵衞佐頼朝、常は頼盛に情をかけて、「御方をば全く愚に思ひ參らせ候はず。只故池殿の渡らせ給ふとこそ存候へ。八幡大菩薩も御照覽候へ。」など、度々誓状を以て申されける上、平家追討の爲に討手の使の上る度ごとに、「相構て池殿の侍共に向て弓引な。」と情を懸れば「一門の平家は運盡き既に都を落ぬ。今は兵衞佐に助られんずるにこそ。」と宣ひて、都へ歸られけるとぞ聞えし。八條女院の仁和寺の常磐殿に渡らせ給ふに參り籠られけり。女院の御乳母子宰相殿と申す女房に、相具し給へるに依てなり。「自然の事候はゞ、頼盛構へて助させ給へ。」と申されけれども、女院、「今は世の世にても有らばこそ。」とて、憑氣もなうぞ仰ける。凡は兵衞佐許こそ、芳心は存ぜらるゝとも、自餘の源氏共は如何あらんずらん。憖に一門には離れ給ひぬ。浪にも磯にも附ぬ心地ぞせられける。さる程に、小松殿の君達は三位中將維盛卿を始め奉て、兄弟六人其勢千騎許にて淀の六田河原にて、行幸に追附奉る。大臣殿待うけ奉り嬉げにて、「いかにや今迄。」と宣へば、三位中將、「少き者共が餘に慕ひ候を、とかうこしらへ置んと遲參仕候ぬ。」と申されければ、大臣殿、「などや心つよう六代殿をば具し奉給候はぬぞ。」と宣へば、維盛卿、「行末とても憑しうも候はず。」とて、問ふにつらさの涙を流されけるこそ悲しけれ。

annotation.translation: To the question, 'What shall we do about His Excellency the Heike staying here?' the Hyoe-no-suke, Yorimochi, who had always been affectionate toward Yorimori, replied, 'We would never foolishly think ill of Your Excellency's side. We merely believe that Your Excellency has decided to cross the river. Even the Great Bodhisattva Hachiman will surely look upon us.' And having repeatedly made such vows in written form, whenever the envoy for the suppression of the Taira clan arrived, he would plead, 'Do not draw your bows against His Excellency's retainers.' Yet he declared, 'The Taira clan of the same house has exhausted its fortune and has already fallen from the capital. Now it is only through the aid of the Hyoe-no-suke that we shall survive.' Hearing this, he returned to the capital and went to the Jōgan-dono of Ninnaji Temple, where the Nyoin, the Eighth Imperial Princess, was residing. This was because she had been raised together with a lady-in-waiting named Saishō-no-dono, her wet nurse. When he pleaded, 'If it is a matter of nature, please let Yorimori protect him,' the Nyoin replied, 'Even if the world were to turn upside down, I would only wish for this.' Yet she spoke without any sign of attachment. In general, while one might expect the Hyoe-no-suke to cherish such feelings, what about the other members of the Minamoto clan? Alas, he had separated from his own clan. He felt as though he had attached himself neither to the waves nor to the shore. text: 肥後守[6]貞能ほ、川尻に源氏待と聞て、蹴散さんとて、五百餘騎で發向したりけるが、僻事なれば歸り上る程に、宇度野の邊にて行幸に參り合ふ。貞能馬より飛下り、弓脇挾み大臣殿の御前に、畏て申けるは、「是は、抑何地へとて落させ給候やらん。西國へ下せ給たらば、落人とて、あそこ爰にて討散らされ浮名を流させ給はん事こそ口惜う候へ。只都のうちでこそ、如何にも成せ給はめ。」と申ければ、大臣殿、「貞能は知ぬか。木曾すでに北國より五萬餘騎で攻上り、比叡山東坂本に滿々たんなり。此夜半ばかり法皇も渡らせ給はず。各が身ばかりならば如何がせん、女院二位殿に目の當り憂目を見せ參せんも、心苦しければ、行幸をも成し參らせ、人々をも引具し奉て、一まともやと思ふぞかし。」と仰られければ、「左候はゞ、貞能は暇賜はて、都で如何にも成り候はん。」とて、召具したる五百餘騎の勢をば、小松殿の君達に附奉り、手勢三十騎許で都へ引かへす。

annotation.translation: Higo-no-kami Sadanobu, having heard that the Minamoto were waiting at Kawajiri, set out with over five hundred horsemen intending to scatter them, but since this was an unreasonable affair, by the time he was returning to the capital, he encountered the Emperor's procession at Udeno-no-hata. Sadanobu leaped from his horse, tucked his bow under his arm, and approached the Minister's presence with reverence, saying, "This is indeed, to where might he have been made to fall? If he were to descend to the Western Provinces, as a fugitive he would be slaughtered here and there, spreading a dishonorable name, which would be most regrettable. Only within the capital could he truly achieve his purpose." Upon hearing this, the Minister said, "Do you not know, Sadanobu? Kiso has already advanced with over fifty thousand horsemen from the Northern Provinces and is now fully stationed at Mount Hiei's Higashi-Sakamoto. Even the Emperor himself may not cross tonight. If it were merely a matter of my own person, what could be done? But to expose the Lady-in-Waiting, the Second Rank, to such a distressing sight would be too painful for my heart; therefore, I shall permit the Imperial procession, gather the people, and take them along, hoping to make a proper arrangement." Upon hearing this, Sadanobu said, "If this is so, grant me leave, and I shall accomplish whatever is necessary in the capital." He then entrusted the over five hundred horsemen to the lords of Komatsu and returned to the capital with only about thirty retainers.

text:
京中に殘り留まる平家の餘黨を伐んとて、貞能が歸り入由聞えしかば、池大納言「頼盛が身の上でぞ有らん。」とて、大に怖れ噪がれけり。貞能は、西八條の燒跡に、大幕ひかせ一夜宿したりけれども、歸り入給ふ平家の君達一所も坐ねば、さすが心細うや思ひけん、源氏の馬の蹄に懸じとて、小松殿の御墓掘せ、御骨に向ひ奉て、泣々申けるは、「あな淺まし、御一門の御果御覽候へ。『生ある者は必滅す。樂み盡て悲み來る。』と古より書置たる事にて候へ共、まのあたりかかる憂事候はず。君は斯樣の事を先づ悟せ給ひて、兼て佛神三寶に御祈誓有て、御世を早うせさせまし／＼けるにこそ。有難うこそ覺え候へ。其時貞能も最後の御供仕るべう候ける物を、かひなき命を生て、今はかゝる憂目に逢候事こそ口惜う候へ。死期の時は、必一佛土へ迎へさせ給へ。」と泣々遙に掻口説き、骨をば高野へ送り、あたりの土をば賀茂川に流させ、
世の在樣たのもしからずや思けん、主と後合に、東國へこそ落行けれ。宇都宮をば貞
能が申預て、情有ければ、其好にや貞能又宇都宮を頼うで下られければ芳心しけると
ぞ聞えし。

annotation.translation: In the capital, because it was heard that Sadanori had returned and entered the service of the Heike clan, wishing to destroy the remaining supporters of the Heike who remained in Kyoto, the Great Counselor Ikeda said, 'This must be due to the situation of Yorimori.' Thus, great fear and alarm arose. Sadanori, though he had a large tent set up at the site of the burned West Hachijo estate and spent the night there, did not sit with any of the Heike lords who returned, so he must have felt deeply anxious and worried. Thinking to take refuge under the hooves of the Minamoto horses, he had the tomb of Lord Komatsu dug, facing their bones, and weeping, he spoke at length: 'Alas, how shallow is the sight of the end of our entire clan. "All living things must perish; when joy ends, sorrow comes." These words have been written since ancient times, yet no such sorrowful event has ever been witnessed firsthand. You, my lord, having realized such matters first and having long prayed and vowed to the Three Treasures of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, brought your reign to an early end. How wonderful it is that you understood thus. At that time, Sadanori, too, should have served as your final companion, but having lived a futile life, now to encounter such sorrowful circumstances is most regrettable. When the time of death comes, you must surely be welcomed to a single Buddha-land.' Weeping, he spoke at great length, sent the bones to Koya, and had the surrounding soil washed into the Kamo River. 'How sorrowful is the state of the world, one might think,' and with his lord and his retinue, he fled to the Eastern Provinces. Sadanori was entrusted with Utsunomiya; if there was a favorable disposition, then Sadanori would again seek to entrust Utsunomiya to him, so it was heard that the lord's heart became glad.

text: 平家は小松三位中將維盛卿の外は、大臣殿以下妻子を具せられけれ共、次樣の人共はさのみ引しろふに及ばねば、後會其期を知らず、皆打捨てぞ落行ける。人は何れの日、何れの時、必ず立歸べしと其期を定置だにも、久しきぞかし。況や是は今日を最後、唯今限の事なれば、行くも止まるも、互に袖をぞ濕しける。相傳譜代の好年比日比の重恩、爭か忘べきなれば、老たるも若きも、後のみ歸り見て、前へは進みもやらざりけり。或は磯邊の波枕、八重の潮路に日を暮し、或は遠きを分け、嶮しきを凌ぎつゝ、駒に鞭打人もあり舟にさをさす者もあり、思々心々に落行けり。

annotation.translation: The Heike, besides Lord Taira no Tomomori, the Third Rank and Captain-General, had all their ministers and below, wives and children present, but since such people were not so greatly distressed, they could not know the time of their future meeting, and all abandoned them and fell into ruin. As for whether any person, on any day, at any time, would surely return, if they had even set a fixed date, how long it would be! Moreover, since this is the last day, the final moment, whether going or staying, they mutually wet their sleeves with tears. The long-cherished, ancestral, beloved, good years and days of great favor—how could they forget them? Thus, both old and young, only looking back at their return, they did not advance forward. Some, with the waves of the shore as their pillow, spent the day on the eightfold tidal paths; others, parting from the distant, overcoming the steep, whipped their horses and rowed their boats, each and every one falling into ruin with their thoughts and hearts.

text: 平家は福原の舊都に著て、大臣殿然るべき侍共老少數百人召て仰られけるは、「積善の餘慶家に盡き、積惡の餘殃身に及ぶ故に、神明にも放たれ奉り、君にも捨られ參らせて、帝都を出て旅泊に漂ふ上は、何の憑みか有るべきなれ共、一樹の蔭に宿るも、前世の契淺からず、同じ流を掬ぶも、他生の縁尚深し。如何に況や、汝等は一旦隨ひ付く門客にあらず、累祖相傳の家人也。或は近親の好他に異なるも有り、或は重代芳恩是深きも有り。家門繁昌の古へは、恩波に依て、私を顧みき。今何ぞ芳恩を酬ひざらんや。且は十善帝王、三種神器を帶して渡らせ給へば、如何ならん野の末山の奧迄も、行幸の御供仕らんとは思はずや。」と仰られければ老少皆涙を流いて申けるは、「怪しの鳥獸も、恩を報じ徳を酬ふ心は候なり。況や、人倫の身として、いかが其理を存知仕らでは候べき。廿餘年の間、妻子を育み、所從を顧み候事、併ら君の御恩ならずといふ事なし。就中に弓箭馬上に携る習ひ、二心あるを以て恥とす。然ば則ち日本の外、新羅、百濟、高麗、契丹、雲の果海の果迄も、行幸の御供仕て、如何にも成候はん。」と、異口同音に申ければ、人々皆憑氣にぞ見えられける。

annotation.translation: The Heike family arrived at the old capital of Fukuhara, and the Minister, summoning several hundred retainers, young and old, spoke thus: "Because the surplus blessings of accumulated good deeds remain within the family, and the surplus misfortunes of accumulated evil extend to the body, they have been cast aside even by the gods and spirits, and abandoned by the sovereign; having left the imperial capital and drifted as travelers, though one might wonder what support could exist, even to lodge beneath a single tree, the bond of a past life is not shallow; even to scoop the same stream, the bond of a future existence remains deep. How much more so, for you are not merely guests who once followed and attached themselves, but retainers of generations inherited from your ancestors. Some may differ from the good of close kin, some may owe deep gratitude across successive generations. In the ancient days of the family's prosperity, through the waves of grace, they have taken care of me privately. Now, why would they not repay such grace? Moreover, since the Ten-Virtues Emperor has departed bearing the Three Sacred Treasures, do you not think we shall accompany him in his imperial progress even to the ends of the fields and the depths of the distant mountains?" When he had thus spoken, the young and old all wept and replied: "Even strange birds and beasts possess the heart to repay kindness and requite virtue; how much more so as humans, beings of human relations, could we possibly fail to know this reason? For over twenty years, raising wives and children, attending to our duties, there is nothing that was not the Lord's grace. In particular, the habit of carrying bow and arrow on horseback, we consider it shameful to have a divided heart. Therefore, beyond Japan, even to Silla, Baekje, Goryeo, Khitan, and the ends of the clouds and the edge of the sea, we shall accompany the imperial progress, and thus we shall accomplish our duty." When they spoke thus in unison, everyone appeared to be possessed by a spirit.

福原の舊里に、一夜をこそ明されけれ。折節秋の初の月は下の弦なり。深更空夜閑にして、旅寢の床の草枕、露も涙も爭ひて、唯物のみぞ悲き。何歸るべし共覺えねば、故入道相國の造り置き給ひし所々を見給ふに、春は花見の岡の御所、秋は月見の濱の御所、泉殿、松蔭殿、馬場殿、二階の棧敷殿、雪見の御所、萱の御所、人々の館ども五條大納言國綱卿の承て造進せられし里内裏、鴦の瓦、玉の甃、何れも／＼三年が程に荒果てゝ、舊苔徑を塞ぎ、秋の草門を閉づ。瓦に松生ひ垣に蔦茂れり。臺傾て苔むせり、松風ばかりや通ふらん。簾絶え閨露は也、月影のみぞ差入ける。
明ぬれば福原の内裏に火を懸て、主上を始奉て人々皆御船に召す。都を立し程こそ無
れども是も名殘は惜かりけり。海士の燒藻の夕煙、尾上の鹿の曉の聲、渚々に寄する
浪の音、袖に宿かる月の影、千草にすだく蟋蟀のきり／＼す、惣て目に見耳に觸る事、
一として哀れを催し、心を痛しめずといふ事なし。昨日は東關の麓に轡を竝べて十萬
餘騎、今日は西海の浪に纜を解て七千餘人、雲海沈々として、青天既に暮なんとす。
孤島に夕霧隔て、月海上に浮べり。極浦の浪を分け、鹽に引かれて行船は、半天の雲
に泝る。日數歴れば、都は既に山川程を隔て、雲井の餘所にぞ成にける。遙々來ぬと思ふにも、唯盡ぬ者は涙なり。浪の上に白き鳥のむれゐるを見給ひては、彼ならん、在原のなにがしの隅田川にて言問ひけん、名も睦敷き都鳥にやと哀也。壽永二年七月二十五日に、平家都を落果ぬ。

annotation.translation: In the old hometown of Fukuhara, the night was certainly kept through. At that very time, the first moon of autumn was in its waning phase. In the deep night, the sky was empty and quiet; the traveler's bed of grass pillow, dew and tears vied with one another, and only the material things seemed sorrowful. Though one might ask, 'Where shall I return?', I cannot discern it. When I gaze upon the various places built and granted by the late Retired Emperor Daisō, the palace on the hill for viewing spring flowers, the palace on the shore for viewing autumn moons, the Izumi Hall, the Matsukage Hall, the Basho Hall, the Two-Story Staircase Hall, the Yumimi Hall, the Kaya Hall, the manors of the people, the village palace constructed and presented by the Lord Gokajō Dainagon, Kunitsuna, the tiles with mandarin ducks, the stone paving of jade—all of them, in turn, have fallen into ruin over the course of about three years, blocking the old mossy paths and closing the autumn grass gates. Pines grow on the tiles, ivy thrives on the fences. The terraces tilt and become mossy; surely only the pine wind passes through. The curtains are gone, and the room is filled with dew; only the moonlight penetrates. When dawn broke, fire was set in the palace within Fukuhara, and starting with the Sovereign, everyone was summoned to the boats. Though it was not long before leaving the capital, even this parting was regretful. The evening smoke of the fishermen burning seaweed, the dawn cry of the deer on Omi, the sound of waves crashing against the shores, the shadow of the moon lodged in the sleeves, the various chirps of crickets among the thousand grasses—all that is seen by the eyes and touched by the ears, without exception, evokes sorrow and pains the heart. Yesterday, at the foot of the Eastern Pass, we lined our bridles with over one hundred thousand cavalry; today, on the waves of the Western Sea, we have untied the ropes of seven thousand men. The clouds and seas sink heavily, and the blue sky is already nearing dusk. On the isolated island, evening mist stands apart; the moon floats above the sea. Dividing the waves of the far shore, the ships, pulled by the salt, ascend to the clouds halfway in the sky. As the days pass, the capital is already separated by mountains and rivers, and has become a place beyond the clouds. Even when I think, 'I have come from far away,' the only thing that remains is tears. Seeing a flock of white birds upon the waves, one might say, 'Perhaps that is it,' recalling the conversation at the Sumida River by the nameless Inari of the Watanabe family: 'Is it not the pitiable city bird with the lovely name?' On the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month of the second year of Juei, the Heike abandoned the capital.
